title: Cortes Runs His Ships Aground
text:
In 1519 Hernan Cortes landed on the Gulf coast of Mexico with about five hundred Spaniards. He had sailed against the orders of Diego Velazquez, the governor of Cuba, and many of his men were Velazquez loyalists who wanted to go home. After Cortes founded the town of Veracruz, some of them plotted to seize a ship and sail back to Cuba. Cortes discovered the plot and punished the leaders.

Bernal Diaz del Castillo, a soldier on the expedition, describes what followed. Cortes had the anchors, sails, rigging and iron taken off the ships and then had the hulls run aground and wrecked, keeping only a small boat or two. Diaz says the ship masters declared the vessels unseaworthy, and that the decision was presented as agreed with the soldiers. Whatever the form, the effect was plain: no one could retreat to Cuba, and the sailors joined the land force.

Cortes then marched inland toward the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, gathering indigenous allies, above all the Tlaxcalans. The campaign brought disaster as well as success, including the bloody flight from the city in 1520, but in August 1521 Tenochtitlan fell after a long siege, with enormous loss of life among its people.
lesson: Removing your own escape routes can force full commitment from a wavering group. Be sure the goal is worth it, because the same move also removes your chance to correct course.
source: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, The True History of the Conquest of New Spain
caveat: The popular image of Cortes burning his ships is a later embellishment: the sources say they were stripped and run aground.
